content: 1. Viral load monitoring is critical for early detection of treatment failure in individuals living with HIV. It is recommended to obtain and review viral load results at six months after initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART), at twelve months, and annually thereafter. 2. For individuals with undetectable viral loads (≤50 copies/mL), the current antiretroviral regimen should be maintained. Enhanced adherence counseling should be provided to ensure continued viral suppression. 3. If the viral load is between 50 and 1,000 copies/mL, enhanced adherence counseling should be prioritized, and a repeat viral load test should be conducted after three months to assess progress. 4. For individuals with viral loads exceeding 1,000 copies/mL, treatment failure should be considered. A repeat viral load test should be performed three months after the initial elevated result. If the viral load remains >1,000 copies/mL, a switch to an appropriate ART regimen is recommended. 5. For patients on non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens, switching to a more effective regimen should be considered if treatment failure is confirmed. 6. Adherence counseling is essential at all stages of care, particularly after elevated viral load results, to support patients in achieving and maintaining viral suppression. 7. Same-day point-of-care viral load testing, where available, can expedite clinical decision-making and improve outcomes, especially for pregnant and breastfeeding women. If point-of-care testing is unavailable, prioritization of viral load specimen collection, testing, and result return is necessary. 8. Pregnant women should undergo viral load testing at 34–36 weeks of gestation (or at delivery if testing was not conducted earlier) to identify those at risk of treatment failure and perinatal transmission. Enhanced postnatal prophylaxis should be provided to infants if maternal viral load exceeds 1,000 copies/mL. 9. For pregnant women who initiated ART before conception, viral load testing should be conducted at the first antenatal care visit to assess the risk of in utero transmission. If the viral load is >1,000 copies/mL, infant nucleic acid testing at birth should be considered, where available. 10. Breastfeeding women should undergo viral load testing three months postpartum and every six months thereafter to detect viremic episodes during the postnatal period. 11. Infants born to mothers with elevated viral loads or who initiated ART during pregnancy should be considered for birth testing using point-of-care technologies, where available, to enable rapid clinical decision-making. 12. Research is needed to better understand the clinical relevance of low-level viremia (50–1,000 copies/mL) in individuals on dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens and its association with the development of drug resistance mutations. 13. The role of drug resistance testing in treatment failure algorithms for individuals on DTG-based regimens remains unclear, given the low levels of observed resistance. Further data are required to minimize unnecessary regimen switches. 14. Rapid point-of-care testing for pregnant and breastfeeding women can prevent the selection of drug resistance mutations and preserve future treatment options, particularly in high-risk populations such as infants, children, and adolescents. 15. Strengthening adherence counseling during ART initiation and throughout treatment is critical to achieving viral suppression and preventing treatment failure. Clinicians, healthcare providers, and peer counselors should receive adequate training to support optimal regimen transitions, adherence, and management of treatment failure. 16. Implementation of same-day point-of-care testing for pregnant and breastfeeding women can expedite result return and clinical decision-making, reducing the risk of perinatal transmission. 17. Infants diagnosed with HIV should begin ART immediately to improve outcomes and reduce mortality. Enhanced postnatal prophylaxis should be continued until results are confirmed or same-day testing is negative. 18. Cost-effectiveness studies suggest that point-of-care testing for early infant diagnosis and routine viral load monitoring can improve clinical outcomes and reduce delays in ART initiation compared to centralized laboratory-based testing. 19. Further research is needed to determine the ideal treatment monitoring algorithm for pregnant and breastfeeding women receiving ART, as evidence in this area remains limited. 20. Multidisease testing platforms, such as GeneXpert, have shown feasibility in integrating HIV and tuberculosis testing, particularly in resource-limited settings, to improve diagnostic efficiency and patient outcomes.
